title: resetting a bad proxy backend reads the next-link out of a pending IO it has already returned
live_proof: the fix is an ancestor of the 1.6.45 tag: GitHub compare 1.6.45...0ad4de66ae reports status=behind, behind_by=493; the case reconstructs the STAILQ_FOREACH the commit's own diff replaces
object: io_pending_proxy_t, an object of the worker thread's io cache (cache.c)
lifetime_ender: return_io_pending, which hands the IO back to its worker thread; the worker's do_cache_free pushes the object on the cache's STAILQ (cache.c:135), and its next request pops it uncleared (cache.c:80)
shape: stale object pointer / cache.c reuse / list link read through the dead pointer
allocator_layer: cache.c object cache over malloc, memcached 1.6.45
fidelity: model-consumer, real allocator: cache.c is upstream's file at the 1.6.45 pin through the port's two patches; the proxy backend, its event thread and the worker thread are reduced to the loop the fix rewrites, a three-entry list, and the worker's return-and-reissue performed in the order the commit message describes ('the return call can free and potentially reuse the object if the thread gets suspended')
distinguishing: the stale read is of the list link itself: the freed object is the loop's cursor, so the very field the walk needs next is the one the allocator's push and the next owner overwrite
layer_note: the upstream fix does not touch the allocator; it removes each IO from the list before returning it, so no read follows the free. The fixed arm here does the same

native-fix-differential.oracle: the buggy arm's walk ends after 1 of 3 pending IOs, because the reissued object's link reads as end-of-list; the fixed arm returns all 3
native-fix-differential.note: unit_reissued is 1 in BOTH arms by design -- the worker's next request pops the object either way; the arms differ only in whether the walk reads its link afterwards

spatial.oracle: the sequence completes: report.completed == 1, no fault, the case marker printed
spatial.role: control for sublet: same binary and guest, one difference. An object keeps the alias it was carved with, so the link is readable and the truncated walk proceeds

sublet.oracle: fault at the labelled read probe mc_defect_read, and nowhere else: exactly one fault, pc equal to the address the run's own marker published
sublet.note: the probe reads the first byte of io->io_next after the object was released and reissued; both transitions minted fresh aliases, so the cursor's is dead twice over

poisoncap-spatial.oracle: the sequence completes: exit 0, report status=0 completed=1 count=1 mode=0, no fault observed by the supervisor, and the adapter's own line reports sweeps=0
poisoncap-spatial.role: control for poisoncap-protected: the same binary in the same boot, one difference. Bounded leases and no invalidation, so the freed object stays addressable and the stale access succeeds -- the defect as upstream ships it. sweeps=0 is part of the oracle: a control that swept would be a second protected arm under the control's name

poisoncap-protected.oracle: fault at the labelled read probe mc_defect_read, observed from outside: SIGPROT with si_code PROT_CHERI_TAG, and the faulting address and the PC both equal to the address the supervisor resolved from the child's ELF and memory map
poisoncap-protected.note: si_code separates the platform's two refusals and only one of them is this arm: 3 is an access to a granule that is poisoned but not yet swept, with the capability still tagged; 2 is an access through an alias the sweep revoked. The platform's own controls produce both in the same boot

native-detect.requires: the object never reaches free(), so ASan has no event; the reissue is an ordinary live object to it

cheribsd-revocation.target: stock CheriBSD purecap with libc revocation on
cheribsd-revocation.oracle: MEASURED 2026-10-06 on this host: the sequence COMPLETES. exit=0, completed=1, object_reuses=1, chunk_reuses=0. Not caught. The reuse counters are the point: the storage really was handed back out, which is the situation revocation would have to catch if the memory reached free(). It does not -- cache.c keeps it on its own STAILQ and slabs.c returns it to the page, so libc's quarantine never holds it.
cheribsd-revocation.control: the control fired in the SAME boot: revocation-control exit=162 signal=34 (SIGPROT) si_code=2 (PROT_CHERI_TAG) with pc == the address the supervisor resolved independently (0x101e42). The platform controls cheribsd-abi and cheribsd-bounds passed in the same run.
cheribsd-revocation.platform: stock CheriBSD purecap built on this host with tests/cheri-baseline/provision-cheri-vehicle.sh (kernel CHERI-PURECAP-QEMU, releng/26.07-88f39900c329 = pins.env's CHERIBSD_REV; hw.machine_arch riscv64c; qemu 16135483052dfdd6, firmware f0e1fe57b0f85075, kernel 8ab453f46dc76cf2, libc fdce2289224bb519, image 0cb16209c16c5edf). NOT the PoisonCap platform the 2026-09-21 bundles used, so those hashes differ by construction.

note: damage is the walk ending early: upstream reports a crash, because the reused object's link is whatever its new owner wrote there; the reduction's new owner zeroes it, which reads as end-of-list. The consequence differs, the stale read is the same
